contents.text: Have you ever felt heat from a fireplace? Or the warm rays of the Sun? Then you've encountered infrared waves! Infrared waves are a type of electromagnetic wave. We cannot see infrared waves, but they are all around us. The unique characteristics of infrared waves have led to their use in TV remote controls, thermal imaging cameras, and devices that monitor Earth and space.
This model shows different types of electromagnetic waves.

subheader.text: Compare the wavelengths of visible light and infrared waves.

subpoints.text: As you move from left to right on this model of the electromagnetic spectrum, wavelength decreases. Infrared waves are to the left of visible light. So, visible light has a shorter wavelength.

subheader.text: Compare the frequencies of visible light and infrared waves.

subpoints.text: The longer the wavelength of an electromagnetic wave, the lower its frequency. So, visible light has a higher frequency.

subheader.text: Compare the energy of visible light and infrared waves.

subpoints.text: As you move from left to right on this model of the electromagnetic spectrum, frequency increases. The higher the frequency of an electromagnetic wave, the more energy it carries. So, visible light carries more energy than infrared waves.

textContent.text: While visiting his grandparents, Mateo used his phone to play them a new album by his favorite musician. Smiling, his grandparents pulled out an old record player from their closet to show him some music from when they were young. While their rock 'n' roll music was enjoyable, the record player itself really caught Mateo's attention. How does a tiny needle on a spinning disk make music?

pieces.text: Records are disks made of a plastic called

. Sounds are recorded on vinyl in a series of microscopic grooves. When a record player's needle moves across the grooves, it shifts up and down thousands of times a second. This produces vibrations that can be amplified to play the recorded song.

imageLabel.text: A needle moves over a record's grooves.

pieces.text: The pattern in a vinyl record's grooves is an example of a

—a way to encode information. Record grooves encode a song's information by changing the needle's path to match the recorded sound wave's shape. Because the grooves are not perfectly straight, the needle vibrates as it moves along the path. These vibrations match the original sound wave, which can then be played through a speaker.

imageLabel.text: A close-up of a record's grooves

pieces.text: The type of signal a record uses is an
. Analog signals encode information by using a representation, or analogy, of the information. They are made of

data. For example, a record's grooves are a physical representation of a recorded sound wave. The grooves form a smooth, unbroken wave that corresponds exactly to how the recorded sound changes over time.

textContent.text: This is a model of an analog signal.

alternativeText.text: A model of an analog signal. A wave with a pattern of high peaks and low valleys is shown from left to right. Below the wave, there is an arrow labeled "time" that points from left to right.

textContent.text: Just like a record's grooves, other analog signals can encode information. For example, a radio station encodes sound through radio waves. Like light, radio waves are a type of electromagnetic wave, but we cannot see them. The sound waves being broadcast are represented by analogous radio waves that are continuous, smooth, and change to match the original sound waves. Once radio waves are transmitted to a radio's receiver, the radio transforms them into sound waves to be heard by a listener.

textContent.text: While visiting his grandparents, Mateo used his phone to play them a new album by his favorite musician. Smiling, his grandparents pulled out an old record player from their closet to show him some music from when they were young. While their rock 'n' roll music was enjoyable, the record player itself really caught Mateo's attention. How does a tiny needle on a spinning disk make music?

pieces.text: Records are disks made of a plastic called

. Sounds are recorded on vinyl in a series of microscopic grooves. When a record player's needle moves across the grooves, it shifts up and down thousands of times a second. This produces vibrations that can be amplified to play the recorded song.

imageLabel.text: A needle moves over a record's grooves.

pieces.text: The pattern in a vinyl record's grooves is an example of a

—a way to encode information. Record grooves encode a song's information by changing the needle's path to match the recorded sound wave's shape. Because the grooves are not perfectly straight, the needle vibrates as it moves along the path. These vibrations match the original sound wave, which can then be played through a speaker.

imageLabel.text: A close-up of a record's grooves

pieces.text: The type of signal a record uses is an
. Analog signals encode information by using a representation, or analogy, of the information. They are made of

data. For example, a record's grooves are a physical representation of a recorded sound wave. The grooves form a smooth, unbroken wave that corresponds exactly to how the recorded sound changes over time.

textContent.text: Just like a record's grooves, other analog signals can encode information. For example, a radio station encodes sound through radio waves. Like light, radio waves are a type of electromagnetic wave, but we cannot see them. The sound waves being broadcast are represented by analogous radio waves that are continuous, smooth, and change to match the original sound waves. Once radio waves are transmitted to a radio's receiver, the radio transforms them into sound waves to be heard by a listener.

When the record is then played, the needle on the record player moves along the vinyl and vibrates up and down. The needle's vibration is amplified by a speaker, and the song can be heard.
